title: Crypto & Silver Collapse, Software Gets Obliterated, & Two Stock Recommendations | The Weekly Wrap
summary: Recorded February 5, this wrap contrasts violent silver and crypto moves with software disruption fears. Eisman introduces new Charter and Meritage positions based on future capex relief, buybacks and possible operating improvement, then examines AI spending and several earnings reports.
assessment: The Charter and Meritage theses are unusually explicit about their operating mechanisms, but their multiyear forecasts remain unfinished. Charter later results weaken the early stabilization narrative. The capex-versus-cash distinction is useful; high free-cash-flow yield is not a mathematical bankruptcy signal, and less capex does not directly raise current accounting EPS.
framework_points: A low multiple needs an operating or capital-allocation catalyst.
Separate capital spending from earnings and cash generation.
Watch how competitive narratives change the reaction to good results.
Distinguish a profitable incumbent funding AI from a loss-making firm dependent on new capital.
tools_and_charts: Free cash flow per share and yield
Broadband, mobile and video subscriber changes
transcript_cautions: Local MLX Whisper transcript, no diarization; the host is the sole substantive speaker.
Recorded Thursday February 5 for Friday February 6 publication.
Forecast tables are described aloud; this audit does not claim a separate visual inspection.
Large currency figures and share prices are retained as reported when no matched price series was independently inspected.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman presents; speaker attribution follows the full dialogue.

claims.claim: Free cash flow yield equals free cash flow per share divided by the share price.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Use a consistent FCF definition and fully diluted share count.
claims.reason: The definition is correct when numerator and denominator refer to consistent equity claims and periods. Forward yield is an estimate.
claims.next_check: Use a consistent FCF definition and fully diluted share count.

assumptions: Comparable per-share equity free cash flow and share price.
proof.derivation: FCF yield = total FCF/equity market value = FCF per share/price per share.

claims.claim: A free-cash-flow yield above 20% means investors price a company for bankruptcy.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Model sustainable cash flow, debt service and risk separately.
claims.reason: A high yield can reflect expected cash-flow decline, capital needs, discount rates or a temporarily high numerator. No yield threshold uniquely identifies bankruptcy expectations.
claims.next_check: Model sustainable cash flow, debt service and risk separately.

assumptions: Price discounts future cash flows, which can differ from the quoted current or forecast numerator.
proof.derivation: A temporary FCF of 25 and equity price of 100 yields 25% even if later FCF is lower but positive and the company has no debt. Bankruptcy is not implied.

claims.claim: Charter is not going bankrupt.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Stress debt service, maturities and cash generation over a defined period.
claims.reason: No horizon or solvency test is specified. Lack of current bankruptcy does not establish permanent safety.
claims.next_check: Stress debt service, maturities and cash generation over a defined period.

claims.claim: At a $223 price and $121 future FCF per share, the projected yield is about 54% and the multiple below two.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Test the 2029 numerator and compare its discounted value with current price.
claims.reason: The arithmetic is correct under the stated future FCF assumption. It does not validate the forecast or constitute a currently realized yield.
claims.next_check: Test the 2029 numerator and compare its discounted value with current price.

assumptions: Price remains $223 and 2029 FCF per share reaches $121.
proof.derivation: 121/223=54.26%; 223/121=1.84 times. The cash flow occurs in a future period.

claims.claim: Lower capex and buybacks could lift Charter EPS toward $100 by 2029.

claims.next_check: Model depreciation, financing, operating earnings and share count separately.

assumptions: Capital expenditure creates a depreciable asset rather than an immediate income-statement expense.
proof.derivation: Reducing current capex immediately improves cash flow but changes earnings only through depreciation, financing or operating consequences; share repurchases separately change the EPS denominator.

claims.claim: If venture investors stop providing cash, OpenAI is finished.

claims.next_check: Specify liquidity runway, unavoidable obligations and available alternative capital.

assumptions: The firm has a cash deficit but may alter expenditures or obtain other financing.
proof.derivation: Loss of one cash source forces adjustment when liquidity is exhausted; it does not alone rule out every adjustment that preserves the firm.
